reference.source: Mandell, Douglas and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases / Manson's Tropical Diseases
clinicalPearls: Rat-bite fever has two forms: streptobacillary disease (Streptobacillus moniliformis), predominant in the Americas and Europe, and spirillary disease (Spirillum minus, 'sodoku'), predominant in Asia
Acquired from the bite or scratch of rats or other rodents, or by handling them; streptobacillary disease may also be foodborne (Haverhill fever) from contaminated milk or water
Streptobacillary disease presents abruptly with fever, rigors, myalgia, a maculopapular or petechial rash favouring the extremities including palms and soles, and a migratory polyarthritis
Spirillary disease has a longer incubation, relapsing fever, induration or ulceration at the healed bite site with regional lymphadenopathy, and a rash, but arthritis is uncommon

Diagnosis of streptobacillary disease relies on culture of blood or joint fluid (fastidious organism) or molecular methods; Spirillum minus cannot be cultured and is identified by dark-field microscopy of lesion or blood material
Untreated disease can lead to endocarditis, myocarditis, meningitis, abscesses and septic arthritis, with appreciable mortality
Penicillin-class antibiotics are the treatment of choice, with alternatives for penicillin allergy and escalation for endocarditis
reference.pathophysiology: The causative bacteria are commensals of the rodent nasopharynx and are introduced into humans through bites, scratches, handling or ingestion of contaminated food and water. Streptobacillus moniliformis, a fastidious pleomorphic Gram-negative bacillus, disseminates haematogenously to produce systemic febrile illness, immune-mediated rash and a reactive or septic polyarthritis, and can seed heart valves and other sites. Spirillum minus, a spiral organism, causes relapsing fever with characteristic reactivation of the healed inoculation site and regional lymphadenitis. Both can progress to metastatic infection and endovascular involvement if untreated.
additionalDifferentials: Meningococcaemia and other causes of fever with petechial rash
Rocky Mountain spotted fever and other rickettsioses
Secondary syphilis (rash on palms and soles)
Reactive or septic arthritis of other cause
additionalInvestigations: Blood cultures (prolonged incubation for the fastidious organism) and culture of joint aspirate
Dark-field microscopy of blood, lesion exudate or lymph node aspirate for Spirillum minus
Molecular testing (PCR/16S sequencing) for Streptobacillus moniliformis
Full blood count and inflammatory markers
Joint imaging or aspiration in arthritis, and lumbar puncture if meningitis is suspected
redFlags: Features of endocarditis, myocarditis or a new murmur
Meningism or altered consciousness suggesting central nervous system involvement
Septic arthritis or deep abscess formation
Persistent or relapsing fever despite initial treatment
reference.prognosis: With prompt antibiotic therapy the prognosis is excellent, but untreated rat-bite fever carries substantial mortality, largely from endocarditis and other metastatic complications.
pitfalls: Not eliciting a history of rodent exposure, which is key to considering the diagnosis
Discarding blood cultures too early before the fastidious organism grows
Attempting to culture Spirillum minus, which does not grow on artificial media
Mistaking the rash and arthritis for meningococcaemia or disseminated gonococcal infection without pursuing exposure history
Under-treating when endovascular or CNS involvement is present
references: Mandell, Douglas and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases
management: A beta-lactam such as penicillin as first-line antimicrobial therapy for both streptobacillary and spirillary disease, with doxycycline or a cephalosporin as alternatives
Prolonged intravenous therapy for endovascular involvement such as endocarditis
Cleansing and care of the inoculation wound
Evaluation and management of metastatic complications including septic arthritis, meningitis and abscesses
Echocardiography and specialist input where endocarditis is suspected
Advice on rodent-handling precautions and exposure avoidance to prevent re-infection
